Microblog repost trees provide valuable insights into how information spreads and evolves over time. By analyzing the structure and content of these trees, we can identify key messages, trends, and opinions that are relevant to a particular event or topic. However, manually exploring and summarizing large repost trees can be a daunting task, even for experienced users. To alleviate this problem, automatic summarization techniques are needed to help users quickly capture the main points of an event or discussion. Existing summarization methods often focus on extracting keywords, phrases, or sentences that represent the most important information in a document or a set of documents. One area that has garnered significant attention in recent years is nowcasting, which involves using social media data to make predictions about community-level outcomes in near real-time. Nowcasting has been applied to a range of tasks, including predicting demographic characteristics, health outcomes, and psychological well-being, among others. Despite the potential of nowcasting, most existing approaches rely on aggregating social media data at the community-level without considering the individual users who contribute to the data. This can lead to a loss of valuable information, as users may exhibit unique linguistic patterns and behaviors that can inform more accurate predictions. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for building community-level models using Twitter language aggregated by user. Our approach, which we term user-level aggregation, involves grouping tweets by user and calculating aggregate linguistic features for each user. These user-level features are then aggregated to form community-level representations, which can be used to train predictive models. We hypothesize that user-level aggregation can capture nuanced patterns in language use that are lost when aggregating all tweets without regard to users. By doing so, we aim to improve the accuracy of population-level predictions and provide a more fine-grained understanding of community outcomes. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct experiments on four different U.S. county-level tasks, spanning demographic, health, and psychological outcomes. Our tasks include predicting median income, life satisfaction, obesity rates, and depression rates, among others. We compare the performance of our user-level aggregation approach to the standard approach of aggregating all tweets without regard to users. Our results show large and consistent improvements in prediction accuracies across all tasks, with Pearson correlation coefficients increasing from r = .73 to .82 for median income prediction and from r = .37 to .47 for life satisfaction prediction, for example. This dataset, which includes over 1 billion tweets mapped to counties, provides a unique resource for researchers and practitioners interested in nowcasting and community-level predictions. We believe that our dataset and approach can facilitate further research in this area and contribute to the development of more accurate and informative predictive models. In the context of If-Then statements, semantic parsing involves identifying the conditions (If-clause) and actions (Then-clause) specified in the statement and representing them in a structured format that can be executed by the system. To address this challenge, various reordering models have been proposed, including syntactic and semantic reordering models. Syntactic reordering models focus on the reordering of phrases based on their syntactic structures, such as context-free grammar (CFG) rules. For instance, a syntactic reordering model may reorder a Chinese phrase "我昨天去学校" (I went to school yesterday) to "昨天我去学校" (Yesterday, I went to school) to better match the English word order. On the other hand, semantic reordering models focus on the reordering of predicate-argument structures, which represent the relationships between predicates (e.g., verbs) and their arguments (e.g., subjects, objects). These models aim to preserve the semantic meaning of the source sentence by reordering the arguments to match the target language's typical argument order. For instance, the word "bank" can refer to a financial institution or the side of a river. The performance of WSD systems has improved significantly over the years, thanks to the availability of large amounts of training data and the development of sophisticated machine learning algorithms. The poor performance on low-frequency senses is mainly caused by the difference in sense distributions between the training and test data. In other words, the training data may not accurately represent the sense distributions found in the test data, leading to biased models that fail to generalize well to unseen data. To tackle this problem, researchers have focused on acquiring more data or selecting a single predominant sense, rather than examining the meta properties of the data itself. Furthermore, articulatory features have been used successfully in a range of NLP tasks, including speech recognition, language modeling, and machine translation. Traditional sentiment classification approaches rely on supervised learning methods, which require large amounts of labeled training data to achieve good performance. However, labeled data can be difficult and expensive to obtain, especially for new domains or topics. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various techniques for cross-domain sentiment classification, which aims to adapt a sentiment classifier trained on one domain to another domain with limited or no labeled data. One popular approach is to use transfer learning, which leverages the knowledge learned from the source domain to improve the performance on the target domain. Most existing approaches focus on content-driven features, which may not accurately capture the organizational structure of a document. Corpus-wide information can be useful in disambiguating words with multiple possible tags, as well as in capturing long-range dependencies between words. For example, the word "bank" can be either a noun or a verb, and the correct tag can be determined by considering the context in which it appears. response: Dialogue language understanding is a crucial component of task-oriented dialogue systems, which enables the system to comprehend the user's intent and generate relevant responses. However, training an effective language understanding module requires a large amount of annotated data, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. Data augmentation has been widely used to alleviate this issue by generating new training data from existing ones. In the context of dialogue language understanding, data augmentation can be used to generate new utterances that are semantically equivalent to the original ones, thereby increasing the diversity of the training data and improving the performance of the language understanding module. Previous work on data augmentation for dialogue language understanding has focused on augmenting individual utterances without considering their relation with other utterances. For example, some studies have used word substitution, synonym replacement, and back-translation to generate new utterances. However, these methods have some limitations. First, they may not preserve the semantic meaning of the original utterance, which can lead to inconsistent or even contradictory augmented data. Second, they may not capture the nuances of human language, such as idioms, colloquialisms, and context-dependent expressions. Our framework uses a sequence-to-sequence model to generate new utterances that are semantically equivalent to the original ones. The key idea is to use the semantic alternatives of an utterance to generate new utterances that convey the same meaning but with different wording. This approach can help to preserve the semantic meaning of the original utterance and capture the nuances of human language. To further improve the diversity of the augmented utterances, we incorporate a novel diversity rank into the utterance representation. The diversity rank is designed to measure the similarity between the original utterance and the generated utterances. In the medical domain, NER is a critical component of medical text mining, as it enables the extraction of relevant information from electronic medical records (EMRs) to support various applications, including clinical decision support, disease surveillance, and medical research. However, NER in the medical domain is particularly challenging due to the presence of complex medical terminology, abbreviations, and specialty-specific language. Moreover, medical records are typically written by clinicians from different specialties, resulting in significant variations in terminology, writing styles, and documentation practices. For instance, a cardiologist's notes may contain terminology and abbreviations specific to cardiology, which may not be familiar to a gastroenterologist. These differences in language and style across specialties make it difficult to develop a universal medical NER system that can accurately recognize and extract entities from medical records across different specialties. The development of a medical NER system for each specialty would require a significant amount of annotated training data, which is time-consuming and expensive to obtain. Furthermore, the annotation process requires specialized medical knowledge, making it even more challenging to acquire annotated data for multiple specialties. As a result, there is a growing need for developing NER systems that can be easily adapted across different medical specialties with minimal annotation efforts. response: The induction of semantic taxonomies, such as hypernym hierarchies, is a fundamental task in natural language processing, with applications in question answering, text classification, and semantic search. For example, "car" is a hypernym of "sedan" because a sedan is a type of car. The task of taxonomy induction involves automatically constructing such hierarchies from large amounts of text data. Traditional approaches to taxonomy induction have relied on hierarchical clustering or probabilistic models that capture the hypernymy relationship between concepts. However, these approaches often suffer from limitations such as failing to capture the nuanced relationships between concepts, or requiring large amounts of labeled training data. Recently, there has been a growing interest in using structured learning approaches to induce taxonomies. Structured learning involves training a model to predict structured outputs, such as trees or graphs, rather than simple categorial labels. This allows the model to capture complex relationships between concepts and to propagate information throughout the hierarchy. One of the key challenges in structured learning for taxonomy induction is designing a model that can efficiently capture the relationships between concepts and scale to large amounts of data. In this paper, we present a structured learning approach to inducing hypernym taxonomies using a probabilistic graphical model formulation. Our model incorporates heterogeneous relational evidence about both hypernymy and siblinghood, captured by semantic features based on patterns and statistics from Web n-grams and Wikipedia abstracts. The use of siblinghood features, which capture the relationships between concepts at the same level of the hierarchy, allows our model to capture more nuanced relationships between concepts and to improve the overall quality of the induced taxonomy. This task has numerous applications in text summarization, question answering, and information retrieval, among others. Unlike document-level semantics tasks, sentence similarity faces the challenge of sparsity, where the semantic meaning of a sentence is condensed into a limited number of words. As a result, it is crucial to robustly model each word in a sentence to capture the complete semantic picture. Lexical semantics, which focuses on the meaning of individual words, plays a vital role in sentential semantics. The meaning of a sentence is ultimately derived from the meanings of its constituent words and how they interact with each other. Therefore, improving lexical semantics is essential for achieving better sentential semantics. However, traditional lexical semantic models often rely on limited context and neglect the nuanced relationships between words. To address this limitation, we propose a latent variable model that incorporates both corpus-based and knowledge-based lexical semantics. Our approach is motivated by the hypothesis that by better modeling lexical semantics, we can obtain better sentential semantics. Specifically, we focus on two key aspects of lexical semantics: selectional preference and similar words. Selectional preference refers to the constraints imposed by a word on its arguments or modifiers. For example, the verb "eat" typically takes a food item as its object, while the verb "read" typically takes a written material as its object. Modeling selectional preference can help to disambiguate word meanings and improve the accuracy of sentential semantics. Similar words, on the other hand, refer to words that share similar meanings or connotations. For instance, "big" and "large" are similar words that can often be used interchangeably. Incorporating similar words into our model can help to capture the nuances of word meanings and improve the robustness of sentential semantics. Our latent variable model combines corpus-based selectional preference information with knowledge-based similar words extracted from a dictionary. The corpus-based information is derived from large-scale text data, which provides a rich source of contextual information for learning word meanings. response: Entity recognition is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), which involves identifying and categorizing mentions of entities in unstructured text into predefined categories such as person, organization, and location. However, the traditional approach to entity recognition, which treats mentions as non-overlapping and non-nested, is often insufficient to capture the complexity of real-world text. In many cases, entity mentions can contain other mentions recursively, a phenomenon known as nested mentions. For example, in the sentence "The CEO of Google, Sundar Pichai, announced a new product.", "Google" is an organization mention, and "Sundar Pichai" is a person mention, but "Google" is also part of the larger mention "The CEO of Google, Sundar Pichai", which is a title mention. Nested mentions pose a significant challenge to traditional entity recognition systems, which are typically designed to identify non-overlapping mentions. To address this challenge, several approaches have been proposed to recognize nested mentions. One common approach is to use a layered or hierarchical representation of mentions, where each mention is represented as a hierarchical structure consisting of multiple layers or levels. However, these approaches often rely on hand-crafted features and rules, which can be time-consuming to develop and may not generalize well to new domains or datasets. Another approach is to use machine learning-based methods, such as conditional random fields (CRFs) or support vector machines (SVMs), to learn the patterns and relationships between mentions. However, these methods often require a large amount of annotated training data and can be computationally expensive to train. Recently, neural network-based approaches have shown great promise in NLP tasks, including entity recognition. These approaches can learn complex patterns and relationships in data without requiring hand-crafted features or rules. However, applying neural networks to nested mention recognition is not straightforward, as it requires modeling the recursive structure of mentions and capturing the relationships between mentions at different levels. Our approach is based on the idea of mapping a sentence with nested mentions to a designated forest, where each mention corresponds to a constituent of the forest. We then use a shift-reduce based system to construct the forest structure in a bottom-up manner through an action sequence. Our system is based on the Stack-LSTM architecture, which is specifically designed to efficiently and effectively represent the states of the system in a continuous space. To capture letter-level patterns, our system is also incorporated with a character-based component. The key contributions of our approach are: (1) we propose a novel forest-based representation of nested mentions, which allows us to model the recursive structure of mentions in a scalable and efficient way; (2) we develop a neural transition-based system that can learn to construct the forest structure through an action sequence, without requiring hand-crafted features or rules; and (3) we incorporate a character-based component into our system, which allows us to capture letter-level patterns and improve the accuracy of mention recognition. We evaluate our approach on the ACE datasets, which are widely used for entity recognition tasks. Our results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on nested mention recognition, outperforming existing approaches that use hand-crafted features and rules or machine learning-based methods. Our approach is also scalable and efficient, making it suitable for large-scale entity recognition tasks. response: Word representations, also known as word embeddings, have become a fundamental component in many natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. These representations are typically learned using neural network-based models, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), which map words to vectors in a high-dimensional space. The underlying assumption of these models is that each word has a single, fixed meaning, which is captured by its corresponding vector representation. However, this assumption is often violated in practice, as many words are polysemous, meaning they have multiple related or unrelated senses. For example, the word "bank" can refer to a financial institution or the side of a river. Traditional word embedding models are not equipped to handle such cases, as they learn a single vector representation for each word, regardless of its context. This can lead to poor performance in downstream NLP tasks, particularly those that require a deep understanding of word meanings and nuances. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed various models for learning multi-sense word embeddings, which can capture the different meanings of a word. These models can be broadly categorized into two types: (1) probabilistic models, such as Multi-Sense Word Embeddings (MSWE) (Reisinger & Mooney, 2010) and Word Sense Induction (WSI) (Schütze, 1998), which use probabilistic techniques to model the different senses of a word; and (2) neural network-based models, such as Sense2Vec (Trask et al., 2015) and Multi-Task Word Embeddings (MTWE) (Guo et al., 2018), which use neural networks to learn multiple vector representations for each word. Despite the progress made in this area, existing multi-sense word embedding models have several limitations. This problem arises in many real-world scenarios, such as sentiment analysis, where a model trained on movie reviews may not perform well on product reviews. Traditional machine learning approaches, such as feature augmentation (Daumé III, 2009), have been widely used to address this problem. However, these methods are typically designed for sparse binary-valued features, which are not suitable for the dense real-valued features used in neural networks. In recent years, deep learning has achieved remarkable success in various NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, question answering, and machine translation. However, the performance of deep learning models can be significantly degraded when they are applied to a new domain without any adaptation. This is because the features learned by the model are often domain-specific and may not generalize well to a new domain. Therefore, it is essential to develop domain adaptation methods that can be used with neural networks. One of the most popular domain adaptation methods is the feature augmentation approach proposed by Daumé III (2009). This approach involves augmenting the feature space with additional features that are designed to capture domain-specific information. Named entity recognition (NER) is the task of identifying and categorizing named entities in unstructured text into predefined categories such as person, organization, and location. Chunking, on the other hand, involves identifying and categorizing non-overlapping phrases or chunks in a sentence, such as noun phrases or verb phrases. Both tasks are crucial components of many NLP applications, including information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. Traditionally, supervised NLP systems rely on manually annotated training data to learn the patterns and relationships between words and their contexts. However, annotating large amounts of data can be time-consuming and expensive, and may not always be feasible. Unsupervised word representations offer a way to leverage large amounts of unlabelled text data to improve the accuracy of supervised systems. By learning to represent words as vectors in a high-dimensional space, these models can capture subtle semantic and syntactic relationships between words, and provide a more informed representation of the input data. This idea has been widely adopted in natural language processing (NLP) for learning word representations, where words are represented as vectors in a high-dimensional space. The underlying assumption is that words with similar meanings will be closer together in this space, while words with dissimilar meanings will be farther apart. However, this approach has a significant limitation when it comes to capturing the emotional nuances of words. Emotionally dissimilar words, such as "happy" and "sad", may occur in similar contexts and therefore be represented as similar in meaning, despite having opposite emotional connotations. On the other hand, emotionally similar words, such as "happy" and "joy", may be represented as dissimilar due to differences in their contextual usage. This limitation can have significant consequences in predictive tasks that relate to affect, such as emotion classification and emotion similarity. For instance, in emotion classification, a model may struggle to distinguish between texts that express positive and negative emotions if the words used to convey those emotions are represented as similar in meaning. Similarly, in emotion similarity, a model may fail to capture the nuances of emotional language if emotionally similar words are not represented as close together in the vector space. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed various approaches to incorporate emotional information into word representations. One approach is to use manually annotated datasets, where words are labeled with their emotional connotations. However, this approach is time-consuming and expensive, and the resulting datasets are often limited in size and scope. However, the effectiveness of SMT systems heavily relies on the quality and quantity of the training data, which can be a significant bottleneck, especially for language pairs with limited resources. Bootstrapping SMT systems from bilingual corpora has emerged as a viable solution to alleviate the data scarcity issue. By automatically extracting phrase pairs from parallel corpora, we can create a large-scale training dataset for SMT. Nevertheless, the extracted phrase pairs often contain noise, such as non-transliteration parts, which can negatively impact the performance of SMT systems. Non-transliteration parts, including function words, punctuation, and formatting characters, do not have a direct transliteration equivalent in the target language and can confuse the SMT model, leading to suboptimal transliteration results. Character alignment is a crucial step in SMT, as it enables the model to identify the corresponding characters between the source and target languages. Traditional character alignment methods, such as the many-to-many alignment approach, have shown encouraging results in various SMT tasks. However, these methods often assume that the input phrase pairs are clean and contain only transliteration parts, which is not always the case when dealing with automatically extracted phrase pairs. To address this challenge, we propose a novel noise-aware character alignment method, which extends the Bayesian many-to-many alignment approach to distinguish non-transliteration (noise) parts in phrase pairs. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach can significantly improve the performance of SMT systems, especially in terms of precision and recall, compared to traditional character alignment methods. One of the key challenges in NLG is to map the input representation to a surface-syntactic structure, which can then be used to generate a sentence. This mapping is often referred to as the "realization" problem. In traditional approaches to NLG, this mapping is typically performed using a set of hand-crafted rules, which can be time-consuming to develop and maintain. In contrast, data-driven approaches to NLG aim to learn this mapping from a corpus of training data, using machine learning algorithms to induce the relationships between the input representation and the output sentence. One of the key difficulties in data-driven NLG is coping with the projection between non-isomorphic structures. Non-isomorphic structures are those that have a different topology or number of nodes, making it challenging to define a direct mapping between them. For example, the semantic representation of a sentence may not contain any functional nodes, such as determiners or auxiliary verbs, while the surface-syntactic structure of the sentence will typically include these nodes. Similarly, the linearized tree representation of a sentence, which is often used as the input to a generation system, may not contain the same number or type of nodes as the semantic representation. Despite the challenges, data-driven approaches to NLG have shown significant promise in recent years. One of the key advantages of these approaches is that they can learn to generate sentences that are more natural and fluent than those produced by traditional rule-based systems. Open Information Extraction (OIE) is a subfield of information extraction that aims to extract surface relations and their arguments from text in an unsupervised and domain-independent manner. Unlike traditional information extraction systems, which rely on manually crafted patterns and rules to extract specific types of relations, OIE systems aim to extract a broad range of relations without prior knowledge of the domain or relation types. Despite the progress made in OIE, existing systems still face several challenges. One major issue is the trade-off between precision and recall. On one hand, systems that aim to achieve high recall often extract a large number of relations, many of which are redundant, overly specific, or incorrect. On the other hand, systems that focus on achieving high precision often miss many relevant relations, resulting in low recall. Another challenge is the lack of semantic annotations in extracted relations, which can make it difficult to reason about and use the extracted information in downstream applications. In recent years, transition-based constituent parsing has emerged as a popular approach, leveraging the efficiency and flexibility of transition systems to parse sentences. However, despite the advances in transition-based constituent parsing, several challenges remain. One major issue is the error propagation problem, which arises from the traditional pipeline approach where part-of-speech (POS) tagging is performed as a separate step before parsing. Traditional approaches to this task have relied on hand-coded rules and feature-rich machine learning models, such as conditional random fields (CRFs) and integer linear programming (ILP). In the context of dialogue generation, the Turing test can be seen as a benchmark for evaluating the quality of generated responses. The test involves a human evaluator engaging in natural language conversations with both a human and a machine, without knowing which is which. If the evaluator cannot reliably distinguish the human from the machine, the machine is said to have passed the Turing test. Two fundamental tasks in natural language processing (NLP) that can help alleviate this issue are cross-document co-reference resolution (CCR) and named-entity linking (NEL). CCR aims to identify all mentions in a corpus that refer to the same entity, grouping them into equivalence classes. On the other hand, NEL seeks to disambiguate mentions of entities by linking them to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB) or mapping them to null if they do not have a matching entry. Traditionally, these two tasks have been addressed separately, with CCR being performed as a preprocessing step before NEL. By performing CCR and NEL jointly, it is possible to exploit the global context provided by CCR to improve the performance of NEL, and conversely, utilize the knowledge base features obtained from NEL to enhance the accuracy of CCR. The key idea is to allow the two tasks to inform and influence each other, creating a feedback loop that refines the results of both tasks. The goal is to predict the relation type for the entity pair based on the information extracted from the instances in the bag. Attention mechanisms have been widely used in deep neural networks for DS-RE to selectively focus on the most informative instances in the bag and reduce the impact of noisy instances. Words can have different meanings and connotations in different domains, and a word representation learning method that ignores this domain dependence can lead to suboptimal performance in downstream tasks. For example, the word "bank" can refer to a financial institution in the finance domain, while it can refer to the side of a river in the geography domain. A domain-insensitive word representation learning method would learn a single representation for the word "bank", which may not accurately capture its meaning in either domain. One approach is to use supervised learning methods, which require labeled data from both the source and target domains. Another approach is to use unsupervised learning methods, which can learn domain-specific word representations without relying on labeled data.
